subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I have one or two questions to ask the minister before we leave this clause. So far I have taken no part in this discussion and it appears that a certain section of the press in my own province is sitting up nights and worrying because I have not taken a stand on the bill. As far as this marketing bill is concerned, if it will improve the position of the primary producer in helping him to market his products profitably, then I am for the bill. But I feel sure that some of our farmers and fishermen too will have to be prepared1 to make some concessions and perhaps some sacrifices if the bill is put into effect in that province in the way it stands at the present time. I am glad however that the minister has declared today that the government is prepared to bring in some amendments to the bill. This I think will justify the criticism that has been offered not only from this side of the house but in the press of the country in connection with this matter. If we get a bill that is workable, it seems to me that this criticism should be gratefully accepted by the government; the country should be thankful for what has been said on this side of the house in having the bill amended to make it as satisfactory as possible.
As I say, if the bill is put into effect as it stands there is no doubt that some of our potato growers in Prince Edward Island will have to be prepared to make sacrifices. They must make sacrifices if the bill as it stands is adopted by a majority of the growers or even by a minority and the rest are forced to comply with the regulations, because they will have to give up some privileges which they enjoy at the present time. There is however one thing I can say for our farmers in this respect and that is that they have always been prepared to make sacrifices personally whenever they have been convinced that cooperative selling was in the interests of all, and I feel sure in this connection that they will be prepared to give the same cooperation as they have given in the past. But there is one difficulty which I see. Under present conditions in that province, very often we have United States buyers coming in the summer months. They look over the growing crop and if they see some exceptionally good fields of certified seed potatoes which they would like to buy they endeavour to buy these direct from the grower. In other words, they take an option on the crop. Possibly the price is set at 75

cents per bushel and they pay 25 cents per bushel down, the balance to be paid when the crop is delivered in the fall. Whether the grower who has been in the habit of doing this will be prevented from continuing the practice is more than I can say, but it would seem that if the whole province came under the operation of this marketing bill then all the potatoes would have to be sold through the one marketing organization.
There is a similar situation in connection with the fisheries. We have some small cooperative fishery unions which handle to a small extent the product of some of the factories. Whether the big dealer who has been backing the fishermen for a great many years and building up an individual trade will be injured in any degree should the fishermen adopt the scheme I cannot say; I do not know whether he would be willing to come under the act.
I may point out that in addition to the potato growers' association, which is a very large organization in that province, we have another quite considerable organization, the associated shippers, and there are also large private firms which advance the potato grower his fertilizer and possibly seed for putting in his crop. Under local legislation there has been evolved a plan whereby these men can be protected through what is known as the first mortgage plan with respect to crop. That mortgage on the crop is intended to protect the man who advances fertilizer and seed to the grower, and it provides that the crop must go to the person making such advances. Personally I should not like to see anything done that would interfere with the rights of these men, because our farmers cannot carry on very well without their assistance. If there are no compulsory features in the bill, as the minister said yesterday, I think it is all to the good.

Marketing Act
a possibility, as the bill stands, for producers to submit a scheme under which there would be compulsion on those under it.
Mr. MaoLEAN: I am glad the minister has cleared up that point because it is a very important one, and one in regard to which we have been endeavouring to get information ever since the bill was introduced. We on this side understood that there were compulsory features in the bill to which I am opposed, and I am glad that the minister admits now that it is so. However, all I can say is that as far as the potato growers of Prince Edward Island are concerned, their produce is largely exported either to the United States or to the different provinces of the dominion. Under this cooperative plan of shipping through the potato growers' association, the work has been proceeding fairly satisfactorily, although there are always some who pull out from their association and are not satisfied. Perhaps the result will be the same under this plan if it is put into operation. But I would like to ask the minister whether in his opinion, if the bill is put into effect and if, say, forty or fifty per cent of the producers in the province ask for the scheme, it is the hope of the government that the board then will control the total output of the province and that those who do not come under the scheme willingly will be forced to come under it and market their products through the organization.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I am rather more
hopeful to-day than I was yesterday because after four explanations and answers to questions asked with reference to what compulsion there was in the bill, at least some hon. members admit that they now understand that part of it.
With reference to the question asked by the hon. member in connection with compulsion,^ whether it is my opinion that if forty or sixty per cent of the producers voted in favour of a scheme they would have control over the remainder, I have stated over and over again that the basis of this bill is the scheme that the producers themselves submit and they themselves in their scheme will state the action that they feel should be taken in that connection.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Is it the intention to have uniformity in regard to the practice among the various boards as to the percentage that will be required for compulsion?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That is in many
cases entirely up to the provincial government. So far as interprovincial and export trade is concerned there will be uniformity with reference to the workings of the board, but schemes may be submitted within a province and a provincial marketing board based on those schemes, set up. The dominion board may name or use that provincial board as their local board or agency.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: So that ior purposes of operation the majority percentage might be quite different in British Columbia from what it was in Nova Scotia?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Yesterday I asked this
question:
Mr. Beaubien: Suppose sixty or seventy-five per cent of the growers of any natural product desire to form themselves into a cooperative marketing organization and through their local or provincial boards come to the minister here with a scheme for the marketing of that product: can the marketing board under this bill compel the other forty or twenty-five per cent that are growing the same commodity to go into this marketing scheme, or can it not? I would like to have a direct answer to that question.
Mr. Weir (Melfort): That is a possibility under certain conditions.
And further on:
Mr. Beaubien: The minister said: "that is a possibility under certain conditions." Are the conditions under which it might happen mentioned anywhere in the bill? What are the conditions?
Mr. Weir (Melfort): They are in so far as they can be set out in detail.
May I ask the minister this question: I think he is firmly convinced that the only way that any marketing scheme in respect of any product can be brought about is through compulsion-compulsory cooperation; and the percentage that do not wish to go in will have to be compelled to go in. Suppose we assume that sixty per cent of the producers of a commodity get together and come to the minister with a scheme for cooperative marketing: can he by legislation put the scheme into effect without the sanction of the province?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The question raised by the hon. member for Provencher is dependent upon so many different conditions that I am sure he would not ask me to give one specific answer to it. I think, as we proceed with this bill, he will realize that every effort has been made to prevent any conflict between provincial and federal jurisdiction in this matter. A province may use a board set up by the federal government or we may
Marketing Act

use one of the provincial boards, as the case may be. One of the big tasks in framing this legislation has been to try to get over the difficulty that is confronting the hon. member.

speechtext:
I would like to get this clear in my mind. If the minister approves a scheme submitted to him by a majority, can he, without provincial legislation, compel the minority w'hich does not wish the scheme, to go into it? If he cannot answer the question,
I shall not insist on it.

speechtext: My understanding is that the matter would be a provincial one.

speechtext: Is the minister in receipt of copies of the various legislative acts passed by the provinces with respect to this legislation, and could those copies be tabled by Friday? subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: That is correct. My understanding is that we have copies of the legislation passed by the various provinces, and I shall be glad to table all we have.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Suppose a majority of the growers of a particular commodity ask for a scheme, and the minority, who have not endorsed it, are compelled to go into it: Are there any provisions in this bill or will provisions have to be made by the provincial legislature to give this minority, let us say of forty or twenty-five per cent, some board or representation of some kind? The reason I ask the question is this: If you are going to have cooperation and if a certain percentage of the growers of the particular commodity formulate a scheme and force the minority into it, unless you give the latter some leeway I do not see how you are going to have any harmony in connection with the scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
If the question my hon. friend has just asked involves only trade within the province in which the board is set up, then the provincial authorities would have to grant any protection such as he thinks should be granted. But if the trade in the commodity produced in the province is to be carried on interprovincially or internationally, the jurisdiction is with the federal government. I understood from his question that he referred to trade within a particular province by producers in that province. If he did, that trade would be under provincial authority; if it is interprovincial or international trade, it would be under federal authority.
(Mr. R. Weir.]

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Practically every natural product which is grown to-day is traded in interprovincially as well as internationally. There is no question about that. There is no commodity produced in any province the consumption of which is restricted to that province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Then if it is interprovincial it is a federal matter and not provincial, But it is not right to say that every article produced! is traded in interprovincially. There are cases in the courts deciding that very point; where the trade is provincial it has been held that the federal government has nothing to do with it. The fruit case from British Columbia is one; that was a decision of the supreme court of Canada, not of the judicial committee of the privy council, and I do not know that the case will ever go further than the supreme court of Canada. This bill is drafted on the basis of the decision in the fruit case that interprovincial trade in Canada is under the authority of the federal government.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Then from the remarks of the Minister of Justice I take it that the claim that provincial legislation will control the compulsory features, on account of the provinces having jurisdiction over civil rights, is only drawing a herring across the trail. While I am on my feet I should like to refer to this question of compulsion in connection with which we had a good deal of discussion yesterday. I submit that we are accustomed to compulsion as a perfectly proper principle wherever it is necessary for the protection of a market. We are accustomed to the principle of compulsion to prevent diseased cattle, diseased stock of all kinds, diseased fruits or vegetables, or any other products coming on to a market. The other day the hon. member for Weybum argued that as his farm was his own he should not be interfered with, even by parliament, and should be allowed to operate his farm exactly as he chooses. Unfortunately he is not allowed to do that. If he operates his farm in such a way that weeds grow up and spread to any extent he will very soon find a weed inspector down on his back. Whether or not he likes it, he will be forced to clean his farm of weeds. Why? The inspector will not be so much concerned with the injury done by the weeds to the property of my hon. friend who has permitted them to grow; he will be concerned with the injury being done to his neighbours' farms. We have the same principle of compulsion in this bill. The purpose of the bill is to prevent a producer from introducing into a market, whether 74726-186
it be the home market, a market outside of the province of production or a foreign market, any product which will injure the market for his fellow producers or fellow exporters. That is a perfectly sane and sound principle and one which is quite common and recognized by all. It is one which we have had to recognize, whether we like it or not. I do not see anything in this bill which goes beyond the principles which have been well established in connection with the operation of our agriculture and other industries for years.
I give one illustration. There was a time when under our criminal law a co-owner could not be charged with theft from from a fellow co-owner in respect to joint property. This could not be done because of the relationship which existed between them and between each of them and the subject matter of their ownership. But in our criminal code the law has been changed and a co-owner may now be charged with theft in connection with the subject matter of the co-ownership. He is not protected from being convicted and fined or imprisoned. We have the same principle in this bill. The markets on the other side of the channel in the old country, in Europe, in the United States or in the other provinces do not belong to any one exporter. He should not be permitted to ship an unregulated product to those markets which will have the inevitable result of destroying the property of his fellow exporters. It is a sound and logical principle of law that the law should step in and prevent that man from stealing-that is what it is-from his fellow exporters some of the benefits which belong to that common market. I cannot see why there should have been all this trouble and controversy about this principle of compulsion with which we have been familiar for years and which is in keeping with the ordinary principles of law.

In doing so, I wish to take up the battle on behalf of the fishermen. To require any or all persons engaged in the production or marketing of the regulated product to register their names, addresses and occupations with the board-

And so forth. Who is the primary producer there who must register? Must each member of the crew register or is it only necessary that the captain or owner of the vessel do so? I take it that the crew constitute the primary producers and if that be the case, the crew should not have to register.
Let me give the minister another case. We have been talking about agriculture ever since this bill has been under discussion. I am now going to talk about fishing. It is an industry which, so far as the maritime provinces are concerned, is just as important as agriculture and, indeed, more important in some sections. You cannot deal with fish as a primary product in the same way as you can deal with agricultural primary products; you must have a different way of coming at the matter. There are too many complicated conditions arising in the fishing industry in the way of catching, curing and marketing that are not common to the system involved in the production or marketing of agricultural products. For instance we are fishing cod from early in the spring until August 15 when what is known as the weighing season comes in. Cod is fished in our section by fishermen under wages, with the captain in charge. But after the weighing season begins, August 15, men go on half-line -until the fall. Now where does the primary- producer come in? Is the man who is engaged by the month the primary producer, or is it the owner or captain of the vessel, who is responsible for the fishing? When they are on half-line the sailor would be the primary producer. He is no longer engaged by the month; he is engaged on half-line-that is to get one-half the product. He is really as much a primary producer as the captain who owns the vessel; there is no distinction. Will you require the sailor, the man fishing under wages, to register under this act? Then take in our inshore fishermen, or those who fish for lobsters. The traps are provided by the owner of the cannery. I do not think the hon. gentleman would put it as he does if he had any sense, and I think the fishermen have as much sense as the hon. member as far as their calling is concerned. Having made that reply let me go a step further and say that twenty-five or thirty years ago there was in the county of Gloucester hardly a fisherman fishing the deep sea that owned the vessel in which he did his fishing. Those vessels were all owned by the wholesale merchants. But these people have progressed, and in the last fifteen years, so far as deep sea fishing
Marketing Act

is concerned, have become the owners of their craft. That does not apply to the inshore fishing that I referred to a little while ago, the lobster fishing and so on. And they in turn engage men as sailors, hire them by the month to run their vessels and fish for them, the proprietors being the captains of the vessels. They have been able to get clear of the drudgery, the slavery that they were subjected to some twenty-five years ago. But when they come to sell their product the sale is regulated by the men who buy wholesale, it cannot be otherwise under this bill. I claim that these wholesalers can organize a scheme as primary producers under this bill and take advantage of the real fishermen, and in that way the real fishermen, who to my mind should be called the primary producers, will be once more subjected to the trials and tribulations that they suffered in years gone by.
While I am on my feet let me say that I am in favour of cooperative marketing. I am not going to talk about the compulsion clauses of this bill, but this is compulsory cooperation, to which I am opposed. In my county we started a cooperative society by which our people were instructed each year in the curing of fish and the securing of markets. In 1928 and 1929 the dominion government, favouring voluntary cooperative marketing, voted a sum of money which was expended by appointed officials who went through the maritime provinces getting the fishermen together to form cooperative societies, and these fishermen were given instruction in the curing of fish. At the same time the government had expert fishermen working in the county of Gaspe, along the Gaspe coast and in the counties of northern New Brunswick as well as the Magdalen islands, teaching our fishermen how to cure fish so that they would be of uniform quality. To-day what is known as the Gaspe cure or the Gaspe cut of codfish has enhanced the value of the codfish industry of the maritime provinces. At that time the Liberal government encouraged cooperation, not compulsory but voluntary cooperation, and wherever such cooperation was established we have had good results. We can have good results to-day if the government of this country will carry on the work that was started in 1928.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I entirely agree with what the hon. member for Gloucester has said with regard to the fishing industry, and if he looks up Hansard he will see that I visualized the situation when I first spoke on the bill some two weeks ago. I do not believe the bill fits in with the fishing industry so that it

could be applied; I doubt very much whether the fishing industry was in the mind of the minister when the bill was framed. The hon. member for Gloucester has said that he does not believe the act can be made workable with regard to the fishing industry, and I do not know that this is not the best thing about the bill so far as the fishing industry is concerned, because I believe it will only work against the interests of what I would call the common, ordinary fishermen. It lends itself to manipulation by those interested only in marketing; it almost invites it. I need not go into details-

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: When the hon. member refers to fishermen does he mean men fishing on their own, small fishermen on their own?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I refer to the men who actually catch the fish.

speechtext: As labourers or on their own?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Sometimes they are entirely on their own; sometimes they have cannery gear on shares but not leased, as the hon. member for East Edmonton said. They do not lease the boat; the cannery lends the boat to them on shares. They are the men to whom I refer, the men who catch fish individually, whether they own their own boats or whether they use cannery gear. Those are the men who are not going to enter into this picture. There is every opportunity for a board to be formed having regard to the interests of the marketing end only, and I will give an illustration that has come to my notice.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend for a moment? Surely he agrees that even * though a boat is loaned to a fisherman, if the catch belongs either wholly or in part to the fisherman so that he can sell it and get the money for it, then he is a producer; the fish are the product of his work, and he comes within the bill.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Certainly he is a producer; I do not deny that, but I say he will not get a look in. That is the point. The scheme will be over his head; he will not be invited,- he will be told. That is what will happen to him. I was about to give an illustration;
I need not name the province, though I suppose there is no reason why I should not do so. Here is a provincial marketing board that has been set up already, and how is it constituted? One member is the deputy minister of agriculture; naturally he is associated with

Marketing Act
fanning rather than with fishing. Of the other two members one is the president of a big fish canning company-a very worthy man, no doubt, but still the president of a fish canning company-and the other is a commission merchant. Considering the place from which that gentleman comes I think the chances are that his commission business is connected with the sale of fish. So on this board we have a man ignorant of the fishing business and two men whose interests lie in the marketing of the product rather than in the industry itself. That is only an illustration I happen to pick up, but that is how it is going to work out right along.
To go back to what I wanted to say, Mr Chairman, we now have it stated by the opposition and admitted by the government that this act contains compulsory features. I do not know why on earth there was so much delay in admitting that fact, because to anyone reading the bill it was quite obvious that compulsion was there or it would not be worth the paper on which it was written. Personally I am not nearly so much afraid of the compulsory features as my hon. friends to the right are. I have seen cases where it might be necessary for the majority to exercise some compulsion over the minority. I am not so much afraid of that feature, but I am very much afraid of the way in which these men will be appointed who will exercise these very extensive powers. That is the danger of the situation. The hon. member for Pro-vencher spoke of sixty per cent and forty per cent of the producers. The British act says there must be two-thirds in favour, which would be 66i per cent. Considering the different conditions in this country I would go further and make it seventy-five per cent here, but there is nothing in the act that guarantees that even any percentage will be required.
Now that the minister has somewhat come down from what he wrongly believed was the proper attitude of ministerial reserve and told us something of what he thinks of the bill and of his intentions and motives, I understand and grasp his troubles more than I did previously. He is up against this question of dual control, which hampers him at every turn. Then take the dominion board. What is the use of talking about sixty per cent or forty per cent in that case? They will be all appointed by the dominion government, and we are not even told whether the board will consist of three or of thirty members; we are not even told what they will be paid or who they will be, though we might hazard a shrewd guess. In the New Zealand and British acts that is all laid down to the very
last degree. As the hon. member for Last Mountain pointed out, there are eight or nine different procedures, safeguards and channels in Great Britain which had to be gone through before the scheme is finally passed, but the dominion board will be nominated entirely by the government. The same thing may be said with regard to the provincial board. The minister says that he feels that he cannot exercise many of these powers because of the British North America Act, they will have to originate in what he calls the local board, and the local boards will have to do with the schemes. In the meantime we have no control over them, and in the end I always run up against this vicious section 9, where the bill after setting out this elaborate yet vague-and perhaps necessarily so-system of constituting these boards, wipes it all out of the picture bysaying in section 9 that the minister can do the whole thing himself.
I believe the trouble is largely one of dual jurisdiction. The minister says there are these two boards, and he will not be able to dictate to any great extent to the local or provincial board because under the British North America Act it comes under provincial jurisdiction. The Minister of Justice, replying to the hon. member for Provencher, went very fully into the question, and finally he said that there may well be a scheme, not two schemes but one scheme, one part of which-and I think this would often happen-would be administered under provincial regulations and provincial authority and perhaps under provincial law, under provincial control, at any rate, and the other part of which would be administered under this act and by dominion authority. Just follow that out and think of two jurisdictions, one in British Columbia and the other in Ottawa, different jurisdictions more or less antagonistic, at least with each uninformed of the troubles of the other, and attempting to deal with the same product. Who is going to sit by and say, with the voice of omniscience:	at this particular
moment and on this particular point of a railway the jurisdiction of the province ceases and that of the dominion begins? There is going to be one grand, enormous muddle.
I would suggest to the minister that he could have proceeded along the line followed in the Old Age Pensions Act. There we had dual jurisdiction and much of the trouble that has been suggested here. But that was got around by the dominion government saying: We will put out a skeleton agreement or a skeleton act applying to all the provinces and this skeleton act must be the basis, and if
Marketing Act

you care to come in, all right, we will make a deal. Of course, the situation was easier there because the dominion government was making a grant of money and made acceptance of the skeleton act a condition for receiving the money. They had no trouble at all with the provinces. The provinces had to agree to it, and they said: We will accept those terms. It was the easiest way a thing of that kind could be handled. I suggest to the Minister of Justice that we might have proceeded along similar lines in this case, and that if we had put forward a skeleton act we could have covered many of the objections I have already named. We could stipulate for a local board composed of so many members, elected in a specified way, and could have said: If you do thus and so, we the dominion government will do our share in cooperating along these prescribed lines. That would have been the price of dominion cooperation. But as it is now, we may have a board in British Columbia composed of three men, and one in Nova Scotia composed of ten men. We may have the British Columbia board elected by the producers, and the Nova Scotia board appointed by the government.
As I said before, I do not want to be a pessimist. There is some good principle in this bill, but unless some enormous changes are made in the bill I do not know if it is possible, on account of the dual jurisdiction, to accomplish anything. In fact, I think it is going to be a complete fizzle, and impossible to work out, and that it will only make us a laughing stock from almost every point of view.
What I suggest is this. I go a long way with the minister when he says that there is need for some of the features of this bill. He could not have made a better argument when he said some days ago: We must have some act to deal with the need for restricted quotas. The British government and other governments have decided that we must cut down on our export of certain articles, beef, for instance. In that case there was some form of negotiations I believe, involving some trouble for the minister. Those troubles will increase. The British government will from time to time simply notify us: You must cut down on your quota of this or that article. But as the minister said, how can we cut down on a quota when we have no means of regulating that particular product? il admit that there is need for an act of this kind so far as that is concerned, but I suggest that it should be limited to our export trade. Let us walk before we run. It is very like seeing a 
man walking along the road. We want to help him, and instead of giving him a team or a truck or a motor car, or even an aeroplane, we suggest that he proceed by way of a rocket. That method of transportation is very much in the clouds at present. We do not know much about it. It has not met with any success. Would it not be much better to start by giving the man a team or a truck to help him along, and then as we learn by experience we could impose more and more restrictions? We have precedents for that, and we could regulate not only the quantity but the quality exported. We have, for instance, the New Zealand precedent. They have two acts, one dealing with frozen mutton and the other with dairy products. One has been in force since 1913, and the other since 1921, and both have been an unqualified success. New Zealand went slowly and moderately at it. They said: No mutton and no dairy products unless it is of a standard grade shall leave New Zealand, and none shall leave without permission, so as to prevent the flooding of the market in Great Britain at the wrong time. Their acts have worked well. New Zealand, of course, is one corporate body. It has not the divisions that we have, with our nine provinces and conflicting jurisdictions. We could avoid all that by following New Zealand's example and dealing only with the export trade to start with until we see how the thing works, and then we could develop it in the future if necessary.
People are asking: Where does the producer come in? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out the other day that in the British act the individual producer is protected. After going through no end of formalities and procedure, if the minority producer does not think he has a fair deal, he can go before a board of arbiters and they will deal with the situation. There are also no less than two boards dealing with the rights of consumers.
How does New Zealand handle it? Instead of having a board appointed by the government, political appointments with all that that suggests even if it is not carried out, they have a board composed in the one ease of twelve members, and I forget how many in the other. The board of twelve is appointed in this way. Two are appointed by the government, but must be approved by the producers. Probably they would be government officials and no one could object to that. Then nine, I think, are appointed by the producers, and mark this, please. Mr. MAY 9, 1934
Marketing Act
Minister; they are appointed by and from the producers, not from the marketing end. They must be producers and elected by them, and the government appoints them on the recommendation of the producers. Having eleven so appointed, a twelfth can be appointed by the government as a representative of the marketing end. That is fair enough surely. Their interests are looked after.
But it is not possible under the New Zealand act to have a board such as my hon. friend from Gloucester suggests. That will be true of the milling industry. It will be true also of the canning industry, whether it relates to the canning of vegetables, the canning of fruits, the preserving of the products of the orchards or the gardens. It will apply also to dairy products. It will apply also to the canning of fish. It will apply also to lumber mills and like concerns. But it goes even further; it will apply to the storing of any or all of the things mentioned under "natural products." A majority of those engaged in the storing of any natural product may present a scheme to the government.
Marketing Act

Once it is accepted in the way I have indicated it becomes law and the remaining concerns will be obliged to come into this scheme or be subject to penalties of both fine and imprisonment. But it goes beyond storing; it takes in cold storage and those who are in the warehousing business in connection with any of these natural products or derivative products. It goes beyond that; it takes in shipping. The definition of a natural product is:
"Natural product" means any product of agriculture or of the forest, sea, lake or river, and any article of food or drink wholly or partly manufactured or derived from any such product.
The definition of marketing is:
"Marketing" includes buying and selling, shipping for sale or storage and offering for sale.
We know now that the act may be used in the way I have indicated. Surely it is going pretty far to ask this house to enact legislation of that kind. It must be remembered that this action may be taken when parliament is not in session and without any power on the part of parliament, until it repeals the act, to alter the effect of a scheme put into force in that way. This is an aspect of the matter which I think may surprise some hon. gentlemen opposite and should of itself be sufficient reason for altering very materially many of the provisions of this bill. The power is specifically given for the creation of monopolies in large numbers of industries, and such power should never be given in this country. The act might well be termed an act to create combines and monopolies. After listening to the remarks the other day of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in reference to the importance of large organizations, I begin to wonder whether it is not the intention of this legislation to bring about consolidations in some of these industries I have mentioned, or others which might be included, and to prevent competition not only between primary producers but between many of the manufacturing concerns engaged in the manufacturing of natural products. subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I am sorry, I did not catch what my hon. friend said before I came in.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I am not saying anything disparaging; on the contrary I was only asking who would have charge of this bill. The minister said that would be decided by order in council, and I was pointing out that it should be some person conversant with conditions obtaining in certain territories. I was talking of the fisheries, more especially with reference to the province1 of Quebec, and I was saying that while my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture is well qualified in matters of agriculture he might not be so well qualified in regard to fisheries. Perhaps some other minister would be better qualified than either the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Fisheries, but we should like to know who will have charge.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: What about the Postmaster General?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: The Postmaster General may have developed a taste for that, because he went down the lower St. Lawrence for the first time last summer. He was well received, and he liked it down there, but of course the fishing industry is a rough trade.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS

Are all these compliments
given because you want to gain time?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Not at all; my hon.
friend knows we do not need to do that. Time is with us in the discussion of the affairs of this country to-day. Your days are numbered; you are dead, but you are not buried yet.

Mr. 'CASGRAIN:	I was just saying that

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS

why we could not work Wednesday nights.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: We have been working all afternoon, and if more ministers had been in the house we might have had some further explanations. Now we have a majority of council here, so perhaps we can find out what minister will be appointed by order in council to administer this bill. I have asked several of the ministers, but they could not give me any answer. Now I am going to ask the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
He will answer you at
once, as soon as you sit down.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Very well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
It is never the practice,
under British constitutional government, to anticipate the action of the governor in council. The hon. gentleman is a student of the constitution, and he should know that.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: The practice is to state in the statute which minister will administer it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: No. That was not followed by the hon. gentleman himself.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: That has not been the practice of the right hon. gentleman, but there is a difference between his practice and the British constitution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: May I point out why it is done in this way? Death does sometimes destroy people, and in order that it may be possible to assign to any particular minister the administration of the act this procedure is followed. This is the modern practice with respect to the administration of a bill or a statute. It is administered in the first instance by the minister who takes charge of it, but conditions may change; life is not certain. We simply provide here that action may be taken in this way.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That is better than the
British constitution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: As to the governor in council, I think my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Justice will admit that it is not customary in any parliamentary institution to anticipate by a statement what action might be taken by the governor in council, because possibly the speaker at the moment might not be a member of that council.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend remember the eloquence he displayed when he was attacking that procedure? He referred to it as the new despotism referred to by Lord Hewart, the doing by regulation or order in council of things which ought to be done by parliament? My right hon. friend was correct at the time, and I hope he will endeavour to make his actions conform to his views and expressions of opinion at that time. I think my right hon. friend was much better when he was leader of the opposition, even so far as the British constitution is concerned, than he is to-day. Power is spoiling my right hon. friend; really I think he ought to go to purgatory for a short time to purify his constitutional soul.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
You know, Mr. Chairman, it is so delightful to hear the hon. gentleman speak in these terms, for his genial good humour so much more becomes him than the other attitude he sometimes assumes. When he indicated a moment ago that he thought I was right in the observations which I directed to the house some years ago I only regretted that it took him so long to discover it. I feel perfectly confident that after the same length of time that has elapsed since those observations were made and to-day, he will realize that I am right now. I have no doubt as to that.
I am sure my hon. friend does not desire to confuse this matter with that with which Lord Hewart was dealing. He was dealing with a statute which conferred upon the governor in council the power to legislate, and he said that was going too far. Chief Justice Mulock, of Ontario, took up the matter the other day in an address at a banquet, in which he dealt with it in much the same way. Some of the members of the British government replied to Lord Hewart, pointing out that it is perfectly clear that in these modern days you must have large authority vested in the executive to meet conditions which change every day. We must be able to meet those conditions and that is why regulations having the force of law are passed by the executive. I am sure if the hon. gentleman will just carry his mind back to the administration of law in his time he will realize that without this power it would be practically impossible

Privilege-Mr. Luchkovich
to conduct the government. Supposing you set out your regulations and make them part of the statute; supposing we had done that two years ago-

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Naming the minister is what we are talking about.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I am dealing with what the hon. gentleman was saying. I think it would be impossible to name the minister.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Designate him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Designating the minister is not, it seems to me, imperative by any stretch of the imagination. It might be desirable, but I have explained why it has not been done. With man's uncertain tenure of life, or for other reasons, it may be desirable to transfer the administration of a statute from one minister to another. That happens frequently in Great Britain; it happened here, for instance, in connection with the mounted police. When I first came to this house in 1911 the Prime Minister administered the mounted police, but they were transferred to the Minister of Justice for reasons that are quite obvious. I could name other statutes the administration of which has been changed from time to time by executive action.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Is there not a [DOT]general statute which empowers the governor in council to make such changes? Did not Sir Robert Borden put through such a statute?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Yes, to enable that to be done, and in order that there might be no question it is so stated in this statute as a matter of abundant precaution. I do not think any complaint should be made because this practice has been followed. It is not important; there is no great principle involved. It is a question as to which minister shall administer the statute, and the minister who will administer it will be that minister who, from the condition of his own department, might have the best training to carry on that administration with the least expense to the country. That is all. There is no sinister motive behind it, or anything like that; there is no sinister design, but merely a desire.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The trouble is that parliament is unable to secure any information as to what is going to be done. I do not imply that there are sinister motives of any kind, but surely we have the right to some information before giving our assent to legislation of this kind.
